title: Madhuri Dixit Rehearsed for 13 Hours Straight While Four Months Pregnant — and Never Asked to Change a Single Step
excerpt: New revelations from Saroj Khan's associate paint a stunning picture of the dedication behind Devdas's iconic 'Dola Re Dola'
body:
Twenty-four years after cameras rolled on one of Bollywood's most iconic dance sequences, new details have emerged that reframe what we thought we knew about its creation — and about the quiet, extraordinary determination of the woman at its centre.

**Rubina Khan**, a close associate of the late choreographer **Saroj Khan**, has revealed in an interview with Bollywood Thikana that **Madhuri Dixit** was four months pregnant during the filming of "Dola Re Dola" for Sanjay Leela Bhansali's 2002 epic *Devdas*. The details are staggering: a single turn-and-sit movement required filming from 9 AM to 10 PM — thirteen unbroken hours — because the pregnancy made the rotation physically difficult without dizziness.

"She felt lightheaded," Rubina recounted. "But she would never ask for a change in the choreography. Whatever Master ji instructed was final."

## The Making of a Masterpiece

The numbers behind "Dola Re Dola" read like a military operation. Seventeen days of shooting. At least a month of rehearsals before cameras rolled. The lead actors — Madhuri and **Aishwarya Rai** — practised separately from the ensemble dancers, perfecting each gesture under Saroj Khan's meticulous direction.

And Saroj Khan herself was battling health problems throughout. Bhansali later recalled visiting her in the hospital on the day *Devdas* premiered. "Even in a semi-conscious state, she asked, 'Did the audience shower coins on Dola Re Dola?'" he told journalist Subhash K Jha after Khan's passing in 2020. "Her dedication to her craft was remarkable."

Bhansali called Saroj Khan the "Salim-Javed of choreography" — a comparison that, for anyone who understands Bollywood's creative hierarchy, is about as high as praise goes.

## Why This Matters to the Diaspora

For NRIs of a certain generation, *Devdas* isn't just a film. It's a cultural landmark. It premiered at Cannes in 2002, bringing Bollywood to a global audience in a way no previous Hindi film had managed. "Dola Re Dola" became the song that played at every Indian wedding from New Jersey to Newcastle, the one your non-Indian friends could hum, the proof that Bollywood's spectacle could stand alongside anything Hollywood produced.

Madhuri Dixit's connection to the diaspora runs even deeper. After marrying US-based cardiovascular surgeon **Shriram Nene** in 1999, she moved to **Denver, Colorado**, stepping away from Bollywood at the absolute peak of her career. It was Bhansali who persuaded her to return for the role of Chandramukhi in *Devdas* — and now we know she did it while pregnant, rehearsing through fever and dizziness, never once asking for an accommodation.

For the thousands of NRI families in the US who watched Madhuri transition from screen goddess to Denver mom — attending school events, navigating American suburban life — these revelations add a deeply human layer to an already mythical performance. She wasn't just acting in *Devdas*. She was building a family while creating art, balancing two worlds in a way that resonates with every immigrant who has ever had to be twice as resilient to achieve half the recognition.

## The Complicated Legacy

The story isn't without its shadows. Rubina Khan also revealed the long-standing tension between Saroj Khan and Bhansali. Khan alleged that Bhansali's team used her choreography in the 2013 film *Goliyon Ki Rasleela: Ram-Leela* without credit or compensation, attributing the work to another choreographer, Vishnu Deva. It's a reminder that Bollywood's most beautiful creations often have messy, contested histories behind them.

## A Denver Mom's Unfinished Dance

After wrapping *Devdas*, Madhuri welcomed her sons **Arin** (2003) and **Ryan** (2005), made a comeback with *Aaja Nachle* in 2007, and eventually relocated to Mumbai. But for NRIs, she'll always be the woman who proved you could leave Bollywood, build a life abroad, and still create something timeless when you chose to return.

The next time "Dola Re Dola" plays at a wedding — and it will, because some songs are simply woven into the diaspora's DNA — remember that every frame of Madhuri's performance was earned through thirteen-hour days, a fever she never complained about, and a pregnancy she never used as an excuse. That's not just dedication. That's legacy.
